Son of a siddha named La stod dkar po. Said to have "taken the see" (it is not specified of which institution) after Zhang e pa (ID:6660) ([3HXACZSD]: 214, based on the Red Annals).

Based on the Red Annals, this is the same person as the "monk bSod nams rin chen" who authored the "las kyi me long" (ID:5239) ([3HXACZSD]: 214) and hence also the author of the topical outline (ID:5247) and the auto-commentary on the first (ID:7972) .
The editors of [KUYBGM7V] suggest as author of the two works the 13th-century gSang phu ba bSod nams rin chen mchog.

comments:
The "btsun pa grags pa rgyal mtshan" who wrote down (ID:4794) could be Ze'u grags pa rgyal mtshan/Chu mig pa grags pa rgyal mtshan (ID:6133), a teacher of sKyo ston. (See Skyo ston smon lam tshul khrims kyi rnam thar in [LRSRMBWG]: 349a2). 
According to [NTGHCZA8]: 65, n. 145, this Chu mig pa Grags pa rgyal mtshan could be the "Grags rgyal" mentioned in Sangs rgyas sgom pa's biography. In fact this “slob dpon Grags rgyal” bestowed on Sangs rgyas sgom pa (1179-1250) similar teachings to those that we find listed as passed from Chu mig pa Grags pa rgyal mtshan to sKyo ston. The gDams ngag mdzod reports a Chu mig pa Grags pa rgyal mtshan in the transmission of the white Jambhala (dzam dkar) that runs thus: spyan ras gzigs| rgya brtson 'gris seng ge| nag tsho tshul rgyal| rong pa phyag sor ba| pu to ba| sha ra ba| gtum ston pa| chu mig pa grags pa rgyal mtshan| gro ston bdud rtsi grags| zhang ston chos blo| mchims nam mkha' grags […] (the list reaches Tāranātha and then refers to a lineage given previously for the following lineage holders, so it would seem that the source for this lineage is given somewhere in Tāranātha's writings). If this is the case, this Chu mig pa Grags pa rgyal mtshan would be already a student of the first abbot of sNar thang gTum ston grags pa (1106-1166). This would be possible only if this Grags pa rgyal mtshan was born around the late 1150s and taught sKyo ston when he was already about 70 years of age.
name: btsun pa grags pa rgyal mtshan

comments:
Van der Kuijp ([FEHIEFEB]: 143) lists as potential candidates: sKag pa ston gzhon (whom he discards as this contemporary of Sa skya Paṇḍita would have been too old), sBas pa ston gzhon (ID: 6651) (a possible option, although he is not explicitly associated with epistemology), and Cog ro ston gzhon (as the most likely option).
Understood by Sun Weijin to be the "'jam dbyangs ston gzhon" in the Pramāṇavārttika lineage mentioned by 'Gos Lo tsā ba ([FEHIEFEB]: 143).
He traveled to the Mongol court in China in the early 1280s and translated in Tibetan Xuanzang's (ca. 602-64) Chinese version of Śaṅkarasvāmin's Nyāyapraveśa ([FEHIEFEB]: 165).
A "ston gzhon" - maybe the same person - is also listed as the author of two works in the [8H6M69W4]:
- Lam 'bras gyi bshad pa gsung ngag nyi ma'i 'od zer in 230 folios
- Kun gyi sna lam du ma grags pa'i rin po che'i gsung 'ga' <gnyan ston tshul rgyal dang ston gzhon gnyis kyis> zin bris su mdzad pa rnams in 38 folios. ([FEHIEFEB]: 166).

comments:
Born in 1091 at gTsang rong gyung and died at the age of 76 in Zul phu according to [R894SIKE]: 109.
[W4T5ZMUP]: 38 accordingly proposes the dates 1091-1166.
[VKBZTBWN], fol. 3b6 reports that he was born the year rNgog lo (ID:3786) came back to Tibet, i.e., ca. 1092.
On his life, based on the Zul phu mkhan byang chub rin chen dpal bzang po'i rnam par thar pa (ID:6715), see [W4T5ZMUP]: 40.
It is unclear whether he is the same person as rGya 'dul ba 'dzin pa (ID:4193). The [NA9AMDH6] distinguishes two "rGya 'dul 'dzin" - the elder (ID: 3941) and the younger (ID:4193) - and a "Bya 'dul 'dzin brTson 'grus 'bar" (student of 'Bre chen po). In contrast, the [R894SIKE] only mentions one "rGya 'dul 'dzin" (the elder), distinct from "Bya 'dul 'dzin" (who was ordained by 'Bre).
[VKBZTBWN], fol. 6b5-6 and [8VLVHDR2], fol. 14b5 report that he was ordained by 'Bre and received from him the name in religion brTson 'grus 'bar.
A number of the same teachers are mentioned for rGya 'dul 'dzin the younger and Bya 'dul 'dzin but, for instance, the latter's studies with rGya 'dul 'dzin the older took place when he was a retired abbot, whereas the former's studies with him took place when he was still abbot.
Further, rGya 'dul 'dzin the younger became abbot of dGa' ba sdong and Bya 'dul abbot of Zul phu.
This suggests they might have been distinct persons.

comments:
[BKUHJCNA]: 703. Las chen reports that in dGe 'dun grub's own words, he "took notes on [Tsong kha pa's] teaching on the difficult points of valid cognition (tshad ma'i dka' gnas gsungs pa la zin bris kyang mdzad)." However, such a work does not appear extant in either figure's Collected Works. In a possible reference to this same work, Las chen relates on p. 757: tshad ma rnam nges chos mchog gi 'grel pa'i steng nas dka' gnad gcod pa gsan te zin bris kyang mdzad.

[BKUHJCNA]: 756. He studied Pramāṇavārttikakārikā (ID: 3772) with one Yongs su 'dzin pa A bha ya kIrti and performed grwa bskor at Snar thang (ID: 4411)...later, he served as an attendant to Sems dpal chen po kun dga' bzang po (ID: 7089) and heard teachings on tshad ma that caused his aspirations (thugs bskyed) to blossom, leading him to exclaim: "This is the first time someone has made me really understand it!" (dang po rang nas rig chen byas).

Fl. mid-15th c. 
He was abbot of gSang phu gling smad (ID:6158) when the Blue Annals were composed ([R894SIKE]: da lta'i shes rab dpal ldan pa 'di'o). But this does not seem to entail he was necessarily still the abbot when the work was finished in 1476, as the Blue Annals were composed over the course of many years.
He founded the Sa skya pa monastery of Rwa ba smad (ID:7085) ([CCSBSVCA]: 688, n. 11).

comments:
The identity of "gNyag" (maybe a misspelling of gNyags) remains unknown.
It is suggested in [Z5WBK2VV]: 63 that he might be gNyags grags tshul, the abbot of bDe ba can in the teaching lineage of rGya 'ching ru ba (ID:4202).
[VSENG5SZ] identifies the author (apparently on the basis of the name alone) as gNyags chung Lo tsA ba (1013-1070) also named gNyag yon tan snying po, one of the four men who re-introduced monastic rules in Tibet. 
There are other candidates with the name "gNyag" or "gNyags", but their views on epistemology cannot be compared with those of the present author. Comparison remains to be carried out with the views ascribed to gNyags ye shes 'bar (ID:4264) by several 12th-century authors.
name: gnyag

On the dates ca. 1040 to 1120, see [HCLRANG3]. This conflicts with a mention, in the Chos 'byung mkhas pa'i dga' ston, of Gro lung pa being considered for serving as abbot after rNam par ba (ID:6147), i.e. in 1151 ([7FZ3B926]: 111). It also makes it difficult that he was a teacher of Phywa pa (ID:3831), which would have been when Phywa pa was 11 years of age or younger.

In view of the epithet "gro lung pa," he possibly hailed from La stod gro lung (ID:7412) or Gro bo lung (ID:7411).

Fl. late 13th to early 14th c. We assume that the gZhon nu rin chen who was abbot of gSang phu is the same person as the author of the two works by gZhon nu rin chen.
The latter is characterized in [8H6M69W4], No. 15506, as the "student of Nyang" (nyang gi slob ma), which, in view of the colophon of (ID:4625), is Nyang bran pa Chos kyi ye shes (ID:3876) rather than Nyang bran pa Chos kyi seng ge (ID:3844).

comments:
Eighth throne-holder of gSang phu gling smad and 16th mkhan po of the Gling smad.
It is reported that during 'Jam dbyang Śākya gzhon nu's time as abbot of the sGros seminary of the Lower monastery (ca. 1326), there was a split between the old (rnying) and the new (gsar). Śākya gzhon nu's oral teachings were taught in "Old sGros" ([7FZ3B926]: 118).
This, however, conflicts with the dates determined for the dates of activity of the next abbot in [CCSBSVCA]: 686, namely 1293-1301.

comments:
The Abhidharma lineage found in (ID:5483) names "khu lha sdings pa brtson 'grus g.yung drung" between "gar mi yon tan g.yung drung" (ID:4234) and "rgya rgyal bu tshul le" (ID:4238). We consider "khu lha sdings pa" to be the same person as "khu ston brtson 'grus g.yung drung," who founded lHa sdings (ID:6701) in Yar lung.
He is also mistakenly given the name Khu ston shes rab brtson 'grus in a lineage list, but should not be confused with (ID:3823) ([TZC3JQWE]: 342).

His dates can be approximated as 1070-1130.

He is possibly the same person as Byang 'chad khyung (ID:6382), as [NA9AMDH6] states that Khyung rin chen grags held Byang 'chad (ID:4416) and taught Sa chen (ID:4205) there ([647FFPZR]: 543). [CJ75QQKN]: 339 (fol. 8a/170a1-3).
dMar ston's Zhib mo rdo rje ([RA3FK3BK]: 134 and 137), on the other hand, distinguish the two figures and places Sa chen's studies with Khyung at Nyang stod byang 'chad, and those with Khyung rin chen grags at Nyang stod.

On the reference to Khyung as "slang pa/slang pha/slang pha ba" (understood as a regionalism for "glang pa/glang pha ba," see [WL39GVT5]: 940.

According to [K9NNDTDS]: 1397, n. 37, "ngur smrig" designates a religious clothing of yellow-red color.

The majority of the information available on Phya pa has been provided in [EZ5JXHJY] and [8S7FDMCJ]. Summaries of the same are also found in [LQZU66YX]: 37-40, [F4UK2S8P]: 2-3, and [BW9UR427]: 35-36 (in French).


On his birth in 1109, the year of rNgog Blo ldan shes rab (ID:3786)'s passing, see [TM8DW8WA]: 32-33, [VKBZTBWN]: 4b4-5, and [8GL7ZT7Y]: 15b2-3.
On the date of his passing in a "sa mo glang" year, see [R894SIKE]: 400, [VKBZTBWN]: 4b4-5 and 6a5. 
[95UZA9Y5]: 40/3/5 (reported in [7FZ3B926]: 111 and [MPRU5QUC]: 206) specifies the day "sa mo glang gi lo'i nag pa zla ba nag po'i phyogs kyi tshes brgyad," i.e., on the 23rd of the third month.

A list of his students is provided in [EZ5JXHJY]: 356, based on [MQB8JGAX]: 297/4, [KL9XTQWI]: I, 454, [4YEPFBIB]: 340-341, [8GL7ZT7Y], fol. 15b3, [VKBZTBWN], fol. 4b7-5a4.
[FDEWZ2NZ]: 290 also mentions the list of the four "jo sras" from bSod nams dpal's Bla ma rngog pa yab sras rim par byon pa’i rnam thar rin po che’i rgyan gyi phreng ba.

'Gos lo tsa ba lists numerous works composed before Phya pa took the see of gSang phu; these include commentaries and summaries on the Five works of Maitreya, the Pramāṇaviniścaya, the Satyadvayavibhaṅga, Madhyamakālaṃkāra, Madhyamakāloka, and  Bodhicaryāvatāra. He mentions having seen these, the Yid kyi mun sel (ID:4503) and summaries on Madhyamaka, as well as (ID:4505) and (ID:5971). See exX0032026-04-2304-02-58 .
'Gos lo tsa ba does not mention any composition dealing with monastic discipline. 

Śākya mchog ldan ([TM8DW8WA], 12-13 and 32) mentions a (doubtful) commentary on the Pramāṇavārttika (ID:3772) in addition to the commentary on the Pramāṇaviniścaya, and three summaries (small, intermediate, large), the intermediate one being the Yid kyi mun sel (ID:4503). (Discussed in [EZ5JXHJY]: 357, translated in [8S7FDMCJ]: 59).

Four groups of students are mentioned in Tibetan sources (which do not imply that the members of the respective groups were studying with Phya pa at the same time), with occasional variations:

1) The "Eight Great Lions" (seng chen brgyad). Eight scholars whose names contains the expression "seng ge," likely connoting their expertise in epistemology. The standard list includes gTsang nag pa (ID:3839), Dan 'bag (ID:3840), 'Bru sha (ID:3841), rMa bya (ID:3842), rTsags/rTsegs (ID:4289), Myang/Nyang bran (ID:3844), and gNyal pa/dMyal ma (ID:6679). The eighth one is instead sometimes said to be gTsang pa 'Jam dpal (ID:6336), 'U yug pa (ID:3846), or mTshur ston (DI:4315).

2) The "four sons of noble families" (jo sras mi bzhi) or the "three sons of noble families" (jo sras gsum). They are young noble men of the rNgog (ID:3847), 'Khon (ID:3848), Khu (ID:3849), and gNyos/sMyos (ID:3850). The four are listed in [VKBZTBWN]: 4a7 and [8GL7ZT7Y]: 15b3, whereas on 16a1 the author speaks of "jo sras gsum." The four are also listed by bSod nams dpal, see [FDEWZ2NZ]: 290.

3) The "three wise ones" (shes rab can mi gsum) or "four wise ones" (shes rab can mi bzhi). The threefold-list in [VKBZTBWN]: 5a1 has rKong po (ID:3852), lHo pa sgom gzan (ID:3853), Par bu ba/sPar phu ba (ID:3854). 'Gar dbang grub (ID:3851) is added in the fourfold list, e.g. in [R894SIKE]: 406.

4) The "three accomplished ones" (grub thob mi gsum). These are students who later became famous masters: Dus gsum mkhyen pa (ID:3855), Phag mo gru pa (ID:3856), gSal sto (ID:3857). The third is sometimes replaced by Zhang tshal (ID:6409), or is suggested to be the latter's direct student.

Also referred to as "rGya 'Dul 'dzin the younger" to distinguish him from "rGya 'Dul 'dzin the older" (ID:3941). See [647FFPZR]: 541.
It is unclear whether he is the same person as Bya 'dul ba 'dzin pa (ID:3818). The [NA9AMDH6] distinguishes two "rGya 'dul 'dzin" - the elder (ID: 3941) and the younger (ID:4193) - and a "Bya 'dul 'dzin brTson 'grus 'bar" (student of 'Bre chen po). In contrast, the [MQB8JGAX] only mentions one "rGya 'dul 'dzin" (the elder), distinct from "Bya 'dul 'dzin" (who was ordained by 'Bre). 
A number of the same teachers are mentioned for rGya 'dul 'dzin the younger and Bya 'dul 'dzin but, for instance, the latter's studies with rGya 'dul 'dzin the older took place when he was a retired abbot, whereas the former's studies with him took place when he was still abbot.
Further, rGya 'dul 'dzin the younger became abbot of dGa' ba sdong and Bya 'dul abbot of Zul phu.
This suggests they might have been distinct persons.
name: rgya 'dul 'dzin brtson 'grus 'bar

On his career, see [KHA9ZVGP]: 3-8.
The dates 1227-1305 are known from the biography (see work (ID:7016)) composed by his student bSam gtan bzang po (ID:4005) ([KHA9ZVGP]: 3).
His name in religion was Dar ma rgyal mtshan or Chos kyi rgyal mtshan ([FZ6N88AU]: 406) - the name Chos kyi rgyal mtshan is given as his "real name" (mtshan dngos) in a homage by Rong ston ([KM47ZZDJ]: 657 and n. 62). 
The majority of the colophons of his works name him "bCom ldan ral gri," a few "Rigs/Rig pa’i ral gri" or just "Ral gri." Schwabland's discussion of the variants “Rigs pa” and “Rig pa” does not come to a definite conclusion as to which is the correct spelling ([CTQMVBPR]: 2-3).
He was born as the son of a local wealthy headman, the fourth of five sons and his birth is reported to have been foretold by Śākyaśrībhadra (ID:6418) when he was invited by Ral gri's paternal uncle ([KHA9ZVGP]: 3).

A "Rin chen tshul khrims" (ID:7135) was a student of Dol po pa, see (ID:7135); his dates (1297-1368) were adopted for the author of (ID:5271) in [J4L5X9AG]: 431.
It is not certain whether the same "Rin chen tshul khrims" was the author of work (ID:5271) and of work (ID:6991).

comments:
A khu ching distinguishes a "sbal ti jo sras", author of a "'du ba" from "sbal ti 'dul 'dzin" (ID:8084) also an author of works on monastic rules, of a commentary on the Prātimokṣasūtra (ID:3690), and on the Sum brgya ba  (see [5RXEUKD9]: 537, respectively No. 11709 and Nos. 11710-12).

[JUARFJSX]: 71, n. 205 doubts the identification of "brtson 'grus dbang phyug" - the author of (ID:4720) - as sBal ti jo sras, suggesting, rather that the author could have been a student of Phya pa (ID:3831). In that case, (ID:4720) would be a different work from the one listed by A khu ching shes rab rgya mtsho in his Tho yig ([5RXEUKD9]: 529, No. 11509: sbal ti jo sras kyi 'dul ba).
name: sbal ti jo sras brtson 'grus dbang phyug

comments:
The author of an early Tibetan indigenous commentary on the Nyāyabindu (ID: 7165), whose first chapter is preserved in Tangut translation. 
The author's name appears only in Tangut in the colophon as "Źjɨr ɣwie." Because the first word, źjɨr, means "insight" and the second, "ɣwie," means "victory," the name can possibly be reconstructed as Shes rab rgyal ba. 
Many features of the commentary, such as the hermeneutic tools utilized and the persons cited in there, indicate the author was part of the intellectual tradition stemming from rNgog Blo ldan shes rab (ID:3786). 
The author quotes from early followers of rNgog Lo, such as Khyung Rin chen grags (ID:3809). However, in the extant part of the commentary, we do not see him quoting from Phya pa (ID:3831) or anyone after him. This suggests he was likely a contemporary of Phya pa. 
Also, a certain "Sher rgyal" documented in the Red Annals fits with Źjɨr ɣwie's intellectual and biographical profiles - see (ID:7975). Hence, they could be the same person. 

 For details, see [3HXACZSD]: 208–216.
